one_liner: Java embedded store for 64-bit-keyed counters; first-party bigram test: ~82x LevelDB write, ~12x read throughput.
what_it_does: A library you embed in a JVM process to accumulate and read very large numbers of counts (long/int/double/float) or JSON-serialized objects, keyed by a 64-bit long. String keys are accepted but hashed to a long. The API is its own DataInterface (increaseCount, readCount, write, read, iterator, flush, dropAllData), created from a DataInterfaceFactory, not a LevelDB-style byte[] get/put. Every interface carries a Combinator that merges a new value into the existing one (sum for counts, overwrite for objects), so a write behaves like a merge, not a blind put.
how_it_is_fast: By default a write-combining cache sits in front of the store. Writes go into 10 in-heap hash maps, sharded by key mod 10, where repeated keys are combined in memory. A background job flushes those maps to disk in batches every second, so a hot key costs one disk write per flush instead of one read-modify-write per increment. Underneath is a hash-partitioned append-then-compact log: keys are split into 64 buckets by their low 6 bits, and each bucket is a list of key-range files that take blind appends. A periodic job, or the first read of a dirty bucket, sorts each file, merges duplicates with the Combinator and rewrites it to about 10 MB with a sparse in-memory offset index. Reads binary-search that index and scan a short run. Whole files are cached on heap up to a third of available memory, and an optional per-interface Bloom filter answers misses.
when_to_use: Counting n-grams, events or per-entity tallies from Java where the same keys are incremented many times (Zipf/power-law keys) and bulk throughput matters more than durability of each write.
Batch pipelines with separate write and read phases: it detects write phases and defers compaction, and optimizeForReading() compacts everything before the read phase.
Keys that are already 64-bit longs (IDs, precomputed hashes) and values that are primitives or small JSON-serializable objects.
Single-machine data sets larger than the heap, where you would otherwise hand-roll a HashMap that spills to disk.
Legacy Java 8 code that can vendor MIT-licensed source rather than depend on a maintained artifact.
when_not_to_use: You need durability or crash consistency. Files are written with plain FileOutputStream append and close, with no fsync. The cache layer holds writes in heap for up to about 1 s, and writes are not visible to reads until flush().

You need exact String or byte[] keys, or ordered scans over the original keys. Strings are hashed to 64 bits with a multiply-by-65599 hash and not stored, so collisions merge silently and iterators return hashes.
You need transactions, snapshots, several processes sharing one data directory, or a LevelDB/RocksDB-compatible API.
Your writes are write-once or have few repeated keys. The published speedups come from in-memory combining of repeated increments, and no fair benchmark covers this case.

You need a maintained production dependency. The last code commit was in 2019. Master depends on master-SNAPSHOT builds of the author's utility libraries via JitPack and on jackson-databind 2.9.7, with Dependabot bump PRs left open. The only Maven Central release (1.1.12) dates from October 2015 and pulls in Spring 4.1.

integration.form: module (Maven JAR: be.bagofwords:count-db:1.1.12 on Central from 2015; current master is com.github.koendeschacht:count-db:master-SNAPSHOT via JitPack)
integration.dependencies: master: bow-utils, bow-utils-extra and mini-dep-i (all master-SNAPSHOT via JitPack), guava 19.0, commons-io 2.5, commons-lang3 3.4, jackson-databind 2.9.7, lmdbjni-linux64 0.4.6, snappy-java 1.1.2.6; the 1.1.12 release also pulls in Spring 4.1.0 (beans/context/core/test) and jackson-databind 2.3.3
integration.min_toolchain: Java 8 (maven-compiler source/target 1.8); newer JDKs not documented
integration.platforms: Any JVM in principle, since the file backend is pure Java, though the core POM still declares lmdbjni-linux64. The benchmark comparison needs Linux x86-64 JNI libraries (bundled in count-db-run/lib). Otherwise not documented.
integration.thread_safety: Built for concurrent use: the file store uses a ReentrantReadWriteLock per bucket, the cache layer has 10 synchronized write buffers, and the benchmarks run 8 threads. Only one owner per data directory is allowed (LOCK file); if another interface takes the lock, the original logs an error and closes itself.

gotchas: Writes only become visible to reads after flush(), which the README states explicitly. Cached writers block when the heap monitor (MemoryManager) reports low memory, and that monitor can call System.gc().
The first read on a bucket written since its last compaction synchronously rewrites the whole bucket (lockForRead -> rewriteBucket), so read latency can spike right after write bursts.
The default config enables the cache layer (DataInterfaceConfig sets cache=true) but not the Bloom filter. The published numbers used CACHED_AND_BLOOM, which you must request.

Stale docs: the README's ExampleUsage.java link and the benchmark-source links in doc/performance.md are dead because the code moved to count-db-run/. The README's Maven coordinates point to the 2015 release, not current master.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: HyperLevelDB keeps LevelDB's API and storage semantics for a ~3.4x write gain; HaloDB is a general value store catalogued as beating RocksDB and Kyoto Cabinet on fill-random. Pick count-db over either only for increment-heavy counters on 64-bit keys inside one JVM, where in-memory write combining and merge-on-compaction do the work. For general get/put or durable storage, use those siblings.
verified_claims_summary: These are first-party ops/sec figures. The hardware was an i7-4770 with a 7200 rpm SATA HDD and 32 GB RAM (10 GB JVM heap); the JVM version and flags are not stated. Eight threads called increaseCount/readCount on Wikipedia bigram hashes. count-db ran with its cache and Bloom layers; LevelDB (leveldbjni), RocksDB (RocksJava) and Kyoto Cabinet ran uncached with default options. The LevelDB and RocksDB adapters do a per-key-locked get-then-put per increment, no merge operator on this path, and LevelDB gets no filter policy. At 256M bigrams count-db reached 1.12E7 writes/s vs LevelDB 1.37E5 (~82x) and 1.06E7 reads/s vs 8.90E5 (~12x). The uniform test draws 128M increments from only 1M distinct keys (Random.nextInt(1000000)), so for count-db it is effectively an in-heap counter test.
status_note: Abandoned since 2019-10-31, with only Dependabot PRs after that and the last Central release in 2015. It is MIT-licensed plain Java 8, so vendoring src/ together with the author's bow-utils/bow-utils-extra/mini-dep-i sources is the realistic way to use it.
